title: The 0.2.4 aim repair: a mismatch in compiled constants
text:
Scope

- Removed the failed v0.2.3 Action -> Weapon Aim pointer handoff.
- Weapon Aim / Field Camera is again an independent touch control.
- Baseline APK: exact v0.2.3 device-tested build.

title: Text is decoded before the game can draw it
text:
Owner evidence: `1000098213.mp4` shows replacement diamonds in Options values, the Leather Set dialogue and the quest list. The unchanged phone resources store their text in Windows-31J (CP932). The original game constructs strings with `new String(byte[])` / `new String(byte[], offset, length)`; Android decodes those bytes as UTF-8. Once decoded incorrectly, source characters are lost, so drawing-time character substitutions would be unreliable.

This fix adapts recognized resources before the original game builds strings. All original EN/JP JAR/DEX/seed bytes, compressed resource archives and existing scratchpad/save files remain untouched. The adapter operates on newly inflated in-memory byte arrays only.

[... selected excerpt ...]

The other 18 recognized entries are typed tables consumed by original `a.class`. The first byte is column count. Each column declares a type byte and a width byte. Type 2 is a nul-terminated text field; types 0/1 are signed/unsigned numeric fields. The original parser derives row stride and offsets from these widths.

`LegacyTextResources.adapt()` strictly decodes recognized text with Windows-31J and emits UTF-8. Plain resource line endings and ASCII commands stay intact. For recognized typed tables, only type 2 strings are converted; column widths grow when needed, and the row stride changes consistently. Every numeric cell is copied byte-for-byte. Row counts and column types remain the same. Converted widths must fit the original one-byte schema; invalid charset data or schema raises an error and JarInflater retains the original bytes with a complete diagnostic.

The allowlist contains only the known 21 names. Unknown entries, model data, image data, audio and arbitrary binary resources bypass adaptation. A `.txt.dat` suffix alone never triggers conversion: many files with that suffix are binary tables.

Strict standard Shift_JIS rejects extension characters found in the actual EN dialogue and JP dialogue/manual resources. Windows-31J successfully decodes every source text cell in both payloads. This is why the adapter uses CP932 rather than guessing replacement glyphs.

text:
## Independent verification

`LegacyTextChecks.java` loads the **unchanged original `a.class` from both EN/JP game JARs** and feeds it original and adapted tables. It checks every row:

- Numeric field bytes and values stay identical.
- Original row counts and column types stay identical.
- The original game's String-returning table method reads the intended CP932 text as correct Unicode from the adapted bytes.
- The production JarInflater announces and delivers the actual adapted size/content.
- Plain dialogue/manual/UI resource text, CR/LF and commands stay equivalent.
- Unsupported names and binary payloads remain untouched.

Recorded samples now decode as `≪On≫`, `≪Medium≫`, `≪Leather Set≫`, and `Basics: Raw Meat`. Japanese samples decode as `今日は何のようじゃ？`, `≪あり≫`, `≪ 中 ≫`, and the original Japanese quest title. See `verification/LEGACY_TEXT_CHECKS_v0.1.2.txt`.

All title/engine Java sources compile against Android API35. These host tests establish charset/schema/resource behavior; the updated phone render remains a separate owner test.

## Presentation/control observations

title: More forgiving targets without longer key holds
text:
The owner's0.1.3 phone feedback accepts the two-thumb layout and asks for larger, more forgiving buttons with a press that can be felt. Recording1000098236 shows ordinary hunt attacks, camera turns and native Menu/Items use with the portrait grid. This revision is focused on the standalone title.

## Space and touch ownership

The deck remains248dp tall and preserves the accepted rows: Camera left/right, Guard/Special, Sprint/Attack, OK/Center. Movement stays on the left; Menu and Items remain below it. The complete240x320 stage, keypad, native actions, directions, camera, saves and Sprint release rules are retained.

Right buttons use the available half-width instead of narrow squares. At411dp width each face is about93×56dp, compared with about54×54dp before. At320dp they are70×56dp;600dp uses140×56dp. The visible column gap is8dp and row gap4dp. Every face stays inside the deck and separate from the other faces. Menu/Items also use wider cells. Normal labels increase to16sp and Attack18sp where available width permits.

A new touch may land up to12dp outside a pad/button boundary. The closest boundary owns the touch. Exact distance ties use a fixed order, so a gap has one deterministic owner. Buttons near a neighbor do not claim the neighbor's face. Remote unused space and starts outside the View remain inactive.

Ownership is decided on touch-down and retained until lift or cancellation. Dragging over another button or changing a saved native binding while held cannot switch the captured key. A missed touch cannot acquire a button by sliding onto it. Duplicate down events for an existing contact do not repeat input or feedback. Movement continues to update the original non-inverted eight-way mask and neutral deadzone.

[... selected excerpt ...]

A pressed action has a bright mint face, light border and dark text. The movement pad highlights its border and active directions, and its thumb marker follows the captured touch. A latched Sprint retains its green **ON** state; a momentary Attack remains clearly separate.

Fast taps keep a visual highlight for100ms from touch-down so a tap can be seen even if its lift arrives before the next screen draw. Native key-up still occurs immediately on lift. This feedback does not hold keys, repeat events or publish extra game frames. The control View schedules its own short animation redraws and stops them when the flash expires. Cancellation, pause/background and view/keypad changes clear contacts, pad feedback and pending flashes through the existing release-input path.

Each accepted new contact requests Android's standard `View.performHapticFeedback(HapticFeedbackConstants.VIRTUAL_KEY)` once. Movement, held buttons, duplicate events and lift do not generate repeated vibration. The one-argument call uses no ignore-setting flags and needs no additional permission. Android handles device support and the user's touch-feedback/View settings, as described in the [official Android haptic feedback documentation](https://developer.android.com/develop/ui/views/haptics/haptic-feedback). Rejected targets and paused/failed input do not request haptics or show a press flash.

[... selected excerpt ...]

The preview and framework stand-ins establish geometry, input timing and requested feedback behavior. They are not phone screenshots or physical vibration proof. The owner's next ordinary phone play establishes actual comfort and device haptic feel.

title: The clock advances in pairs
text:
The function computes a 64 Hz tick counter, then applies this mask for EKA1:

    static constexpr std::uint32_t TICK_MASK = ~0b1;
    ...
    if (kern->is_eka1()) {
        res &= TICK_MASK;
    }

The nearby upstream comment describes this as an unverified Worms World Party
compatibility workaround. This file was fetched from the pinned revision and
master on 2026-10-19; the two fetched files were byte-identical and both still
contained the mask. File SHA256:
c238fb67cf1bf60f2cb3d76859ef7cb5b461f9259ed7449339cf33c4174e364f

WHY THE MASK MATTERS
The mask clears the counter's least significant bit. For example:

    Raw counter:    0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
    Masked result:  0, 0, 2, 2, 4, 4

The underlying 64 Hz tick period is 15.625 ms. The masked counter changes only
every 31.25 ms, in increments of two. It still represents approximately 64
tick units per second: this is reduced resolution, not a clock running at
half speed. With game callbacks near 60 per second, many successive reads
produce a zero elapsed-tick delta, followed by a two-tick delta.

The original Ashen timestep calculation accepts zero elapsed time. The
pre-change phone trace showed its movement command clearing after release
while the player's position continued changing. Input release delivery was
not the cause demonstrated by that trace.

title: One instruction in the runtime
text:
Leave the computed counter unmasked for Ashen:

    - res &= TICK_MASK;
    + // Ashen-only runtime: leave res unmasked.

The native time provider, timer origin, tick period and existing pause logic
were left intact. No FPS cap, time-delay setting, minimum-timestep clamp,
forced velocity reset or friction constant was changed.

ACTUAL ANDROID BINARY CHANGE
The delivered test used a reversible binary compatibility edit to the pinned
ARM64 native library; it was not a complete source rebuild of EKA2L1.
Exactly one instruction changed:

    Before: and w10, w9, #0xfffffffe
    After:  mov w10, w9

The subsequent conditional select therefore receives the unmasked counter.
This changes the EKA1 result while preserving the existing EKA2 result.
note: The dedicated Ashen runtime was edited; the original game executable was unchanged. No binary is distributed here.

After, v0.1.5-clock-trial:
- 2,816 retained completed-frame samples across 61.757 seconds.

- All 2,815 subsequent captured samples had positive elapsed time.
- Tick deltas: 2,621 samples of one tick, 192 of two ticks, two of three ticks.

- Median observed completed-frame callback gap: 16.678 ms.
- Seven clean high-speed grounded releases reached zero horizontal velocity
  in 321.710-342.649 ms (median 326.537 ms).
- Their velocities decreased monotonically and positions stayed fixed after
  stopping. Two of the neutral intervals lasted 7.484 and 8.616 seconds.
- Floor-contact state remained set through those braking sequences.
- The user's gameplay video and assessment agreed with the measured repair.

The seven release examples require: at least one second before the next
movement press, zero movement commands throughout, initial raw horizontal
speed >=45000, continuous floor contact through stopping, and the first
sample within 50 ms of the guest release. Overlapping inputs, short gaps,
airborne releases and already wall-stopped inputs are excluded. Positions
and velocities are original fixed-point integers; no metres conversion is
assumed. The histories are sampled/retained traces, not every event forever.

SUPPORTED INTERNAL BRAKING EXPLANATION

title: The braking explanation and its boundary
text:
floor-contact state. It also found a path that clears that state before
collision processing, and a zero-timestep collision setup with identical
start/end positions. Repeated zero-time updates can therefore interfere with
the ground-contact-dependent braking path. The old position trace's braking
pattern matched this mechanism; the repaired trace records normal velocity
decay with floor contact retained.

The old trace did not directly record floor flags or velocity, and the host
harness stopped before the complete world-collision query. The full internal
ground-contact explanation is supported by code analysis and the traces;
the specific counter mask, zero-time deltas and successful repair are the
directly demonstrated compatibility finding.

Useful original-game analysis addresses for this exact executable:

[... selected excerpt ...]

The four touch movement/input classes were also identical. The after build
integrated UI Kit 1.1.1's startup/dialog release repairs and extended the
read-only observer; it was not otherwise a byte-identical APK. Both probes
observed the original guest through guarded debugger hooks and added some
overhead. Their similar callback intervals and the direct counter change
are useful controls; this is not a physical N-Gage timing measurement.

Host checks included 180 executions of the actual native ARM64 clock
function over tick boundaries, counter wrap/extreme values and EKA1/EKA2
branches. Original ARM input/braking/setup functions were separately checked.
The delivered APK's observed movement repair is supported by the real phone
report and video. Full game completion, multiplayer, other phones/platforms,
original-hardware timing parity and Worms regressions were not tested.

UPSTREAM IMPLEMENTATION SCOPE
The tested runtime belongs to a dedicated Ashen bridge. Removing this mask
there changes its EKA1 counter generally; the binary instruction itself is
not guarded by Ashen's UID. For a multi-game EKA2L1 release, a title-specific
compatibility option/profile for Ashen (UID 0x101FD3E9) is the appropriate
next implementation to evaluate. Preserve the Worms workaround for the game
that needs it until broader regression tests establish a safe default.
There is no claim that the same change fixes every slippery game.

title: One real fix that still leaves a giant Cloud
text:
## Evidence behind this pass
- `cloud.mbac` contains 3 appearance-pattern groups.
- Pattern 0 contains the shared/base Cloud geometry.
- Pattern 1 and pattern 2 each contain an additional 14 textured quads.
- `cloud.mtra` v5 dynamic appearance data supplies masks `0x2` for actions 0-23 and `0x4` for actions 24-26.
- v0.0.15 parsed that MBAC pattern table but discarded it, so both alternate 14-quad groups were rendered simultaneously.
- DoJa `Figure.setTime()` is defined to update both pose and appearance state from the active ActionTable.

## Changes
- Preserve MBAC v5 per-pattern polygon counts.
- Expand those polygon groups to a per-render-triangle pattern mask.
- Base pattern-0 polygons remain always visible.
- Alternate polygon groups use the documented 32-bit appearance mask (`1 << patternIndex`).
- `Figure.setTime()` now applies MTRA dynamic appearance state using the existing `ActionTable.patternFor()` parser.
- `Figure.setAction()` continues to reset time to zero and therefore now also selects the action's initial appearance state.
- Added `Figure.getNumPatterns()` and `Figure.setPattern(int)` compatibility methods.
- Renderer filters inactive Figure triangles instead of drawing every appearance state at once.
- Figure telemetry now reports `patterns`, current `pat=0x...`, and `patHide` triangle count.
- Corrected MBAC triangle/quad winding to the reference order while preserving matching UVs.

title: The model and the world are speaking different units
text:
## Figure model-unit pass

v0.0.16 proved that Cloud is animated, textured, pattern-filtered, and still projected thousands of pixels across a 240x240 framebuffer. The device report also shows the course/Primitive geometry living in a much smaller and sane world-coordinate range.

Snowboarding's own bytecode converts its internal world translations to DoJa Transform floats with `>> 6` (26.6-style units) before `Graphics3D.setTransform`. MBAC Figure geometry, however, was still being submitted by the bridge as raw model integers. v0.0.17 therefore applies a **Figure-only 1/64 model-to-world conversion after MTRA skeletal deformation and before the game-supplied world/view matrix**.

Dynamic Primitive terrain is intentionally unchanged. Camera convention, +Z projection, Z buffer, textures, MTRA animation, appearance-pattern filtering, controls, scratchpad and report output are unchanged.

New Figure telemetry includes `unitScale=1/64`, raw pose bounds, scaled world bounds, projected bbox and view-Z range.

title: Cloud and the course share the upside-down projection
text:
## Perspective Y-orientation pass

v0.0.17 proved the Figure 1/64 model-to-world conversion: Cloud now occupies a sane on-screen footprint (roughly tens of pixels rather than thousands), but the device recording shows Cloud and the perspective course geometry vertically inverted.

The bridge had an internal projection inconsistency:

- parallel projection mapped `+viewY` to `+screenY`
- perspective projection mapped `+viewY` to `-screenY`

On the device, this made Snowboarding's mostly-negative-Y course geometry appear above the horizon while Cloud's mostly-positive-Y Figure geometry appeared head-down. v0.0.18 changes only the perspective screen-Y mapping so it matches the DoJa/Canvas downward-positive screen convention already used by the parallel path:

`screenY = centerY + viewY * focal / viewZ`

The change is applied to both Figure and Primitive perspective projection. Figure scaling, MTRA animation, pattern filtering, textures, camera transforms, +Z view convention, Z buffer, terrain generation, controls, storage and reporting are unchanged.

Telemetry remains enabled so the device report can confirm Cloud's bbox/depth after the orientation correction.

title: The screen was showing unfinished frames
text:
Polish the now-playable v0.0.18 build without destabilizing gameplay. This pass targets the startup/menu flashing shown in the 2026-09-29 device recording and reduces the always-visible development chrome.

## Evidence

The second v0.0.18 recording repeatedly exposes black/gray/white intermediate versions of the same Square Enix/credit/title frame. Two bridge behaviors could produce exactly that:

1. The bridge displayed the same 240x240 bitmap while the game thread was still drawing into it. `BridgeLog`, `flushBuffer()` and UI updates could therefore trigger Android redraws before `Graphics.unlock(true)` marked the DoJa frame complete.
2. DoJa `DrawableObject3D.setTransparency()` defines 100 percent as fully opaque/source-visible for `BLEND_ALPHA` and `BLEND_ADD`. The bridge had this reversed (100 -> transparent). Snowboarding's fade helper explicitly uses `BLEND_ALPHA` with changing 0..100 transparency.

## Changes

- Added a two-buffer presentation layer. The game continues drawing into its existing back buffer; `Graphics.unlock(true)` copies the completed frame into the inactive presentation bitmap and atomically swaps it visible.
- `Graphics3D.flushBuffer()` no longer invalidates/presents a half-finished frame.
- Corrected DoJa blend semantics:
  - `BLEND_NORMAL`: transparency ignored, opaque draw.
  - `BLEND_ALPHA`: source contribution = transparency percent (`100` = opaque).
  - `BLEND_ADD`: destination + source * transparency percent, saturated per RGB channel.
- Primitive default transparency is now 100 percent.
- Added primitive blend/transparency telemetry for future reports.

title: Text ascent was added twice; the tiny font was ignored
text:
## Evidence from the v0.0.19 device run

- The S25 run is playable, but the Android D-pad, OK and soft keys are materially too small for comfortable touch use.
- Snowboarding's pause-menu selection cursor is vertically separated from the menu label it selects.
- HUD strings such as `TIME:` / `BEST:` overlap their numeric values.

The game bytecode explains both in-game UI faults:

- Snowboarding already adds `Font.getAscent()` to the requested top coordinate before calling DoJa `Graphics.drawString()`. The bridge also added ascent inside `drawString()`, moving every string down by one additional ascent.
- Snowboarding requests DoJa `SIZE_TINY` (`0x70000400`), but the bridge ignored the font flags and always rendered a 14-dot Android font. The HUD deliberately starts the timer value only 29 pixels after `TIME:` and 30 pixels after `BEST:`, so the oversized font forces overlap.

## Changes

- DoJa `Graphics.drawString()` now treats its Y argument as the baseline, matching the DoJa drawing model. Removed the second ascent offset.
- Implemented DoJa font-size flag decoding with a 10-dot `SIZE_TINY` default and basic tiny/small/medium/large mappings.
- Font measurement and drawing now use the same selected Android Paint, keeping `stringWidth()`, ascent, height and rendered text internally consistent.
- Greatly enlarged the Android D-pad and OK control without covering the game viewport.
- Enlarged the game-driven soft-key pills and label text.
- Increased invisible touch margins beyond the visible controls.
- D-pad overlap now resolves to the nearest cardinal button rather than depending on hit-test order.

title: The arrows were edging; 4 and 6 were turning
text:
## Why the old control layout felt wrong

The game's packaged help defines the original Button scheme as:

- 4 / 6 = Turn Left / Turn Right
- Up (or 2) = Kick
- Down (or 8) = Slow Down
- Confirm (or 5) = Jump / Spin Jump
- D-pad Left (or 1) = Left Edge Control
- D-pad Right (or 3) = Right Edge Control

The previous bridge exposed D-pad Left/Right as the main steering control, which meant the primary touch arrows were sending edge-control commands rather than the game's actual 4/6 turning commands.

[... selected excerpt ...]

- Added DoJa numeric key masks for KEY_4 and KEY_6 using the official Display key codes (0x04 and 0x06).
- Replaced the four separate game-direction circles with one large drag-style virtual control pad.
- During active racing (`Retry / Menu` soft labels):
  - drag left/right -> numeric 4/6 actual turning,
  - drag up -> Kick,
  - drag down -> Slow Down,
  - diagonals combine turn + kick/slow in one touch.
- Added a large JUMP button (Confirm/5 behavior).
- Added separate large EDGE L / EDGE R buttons for the original D-pad edge-control actions.
- Preserved Retry/Menu soft keys below the gameplay controls.
- Outside an active race the same left pad automatically becomes a normal cardinal D-pad, so menus/config/help remain navigable.
- Multi-touch remains supported so steering + Jump/Edge inputs can be combined.
- Diagnostics now label numeric steering input as TURN_L / TURN_R.

## Intentionally unchanged

- v0.0.20 font/text corrections.
- All 3D, animation, texture, camera, presentation-buffer and fade behavior.
- Audio remains the existing MLD stub in this build; audio is the next runtime target after confirming the corrected original steering inputs on-device.

title: A recognizable silhouette, produced by the wrong transform
text:
Observed on-device in v0.2.3:
- The white Figure output became unmistakably Rockman/Mega-Man shaped when the experimental object*view composition was rendered.
- The shape remained oversized and moved in/out of the viewport as the game camera changed.
- Runtime remained healthy: 1239 frames, 16542 draw calls, 0 GL errors, 0 caught game exceptions.
- At one late camera pose, object*view put only selected body parts inside the frustum (72v arm 8/72, 132v leg 83/132, helmet/chest 0), matching the partial silhouette seen on screen.

Reassessment:
- Official DoJa Graphics3D transform semantics compose the current view transform with the supplied object transform as view*object.
- The preserved Android host's Transform.lookAt implementation is already OpenGL-style -Z-forward. Therefore the bridge's extra DoJa +Z -> GLES -Z flip double-converts this host camera.
- The game DEX constructs the gameplay camera from the matrix translation and forward/up basis, so the camera translation is game-world state rather than an arbitrary renderer offset.
- At the v0.2.3 late pose, inverse(view) puts the camera at approximately [7.0, 4.1, 101.3] and the Rockman object origin at approximately [8.75, 0, 98.41], only about 4.9 world units apart.
- Decoded bind-pose Rockman body data spans roughly 187 raw model units vertically. A 187-unit character cannot plausibly sit only ~5 world units from a third-person camera and fit the 60-degree view.

Conclusion:
The v0.2.3 object*view experiment was useful because it accidentally pushed raw model coordinates much farther from the camera and exposed a recognizable silhouette. It is not the final composition rule. The evidence now points to an implicit model-unit conversion missing from the MB/MBA/MBAC bridge path.

title: The stage has 3,241 vertices and 2,497 triangles
text:
1. The Area 5 D4D structure is valid: 57/57 objects, section checksums match.
2. Object 52 is a 3241-entry signed-short XYZ array. Descriptor object 55 stores position ref 53 (serialized object id 52), bias [-12,16.25,7], and float scale 0.00311288796. This yields world bounds approximately X[-96,72], Y[-0.5,33], Z[-95,109], strongly indicating dequantized stage coordinates rather than arbitrary raw shorts.
3. The eight type-0x0B records have declaredCount values all divisible by three. For 0x82 records, dataBytes == declaredCount*2 + (declaredCount/3)*4 + 4. For 0x81 records, dataBytes == declaredCount + (declaredCount/3)*4 + 4. Therefore the first declaredCount values are the actual vertex-index stream and the remainder is per-face metadata plus a four-byte trailer.
4. Total topology is 7491 indices = 2497 triangles. v0.3.1 showed all u16 index-stream values in the 0x82 records fit the 3241-vertex array, including an observed maximum of 3240.
5. Render those dequantized positions and only the declared index prefix as an untextured world mesh through Rockman's existing GLES/full-frame-composite path. Do not change Figure rendering or force Snowboard's software +Z convention onto Rockman's device-proven GLES camera path.

title: Monster Hunter lessons enter Rockman’s mesh pass
text:
## Why this build exists
v0.3.2 proved that Area 5's decoded D4D world mesh is live on-device: 3,241 vertices, 2,497 triangles, eight topology records, no GL errors, and full-frame GPU presentation. Visually, however, the entire stage used one flat color, so correct geometry and incorrect giant polygons were hard to distinguish.

Monster Hunter i v0.0.7 independently reinforced two lessons for the shared DoJa 3D work: surface orientation/backface behavior matters, and near-plane handling needs to be measured rather than guessed. This build borrows those lessons without transplanting Monster Hunter-specific game code.

## Changes
- Preserves the v0.3.2 D4D decode, world coordinates, camera path, Figure renderer, audio, controls, and GL-to-Android presentation bridge.
- Keeps all eight D4D topology streams separate through rendering instead of flattening them into one index buffer draw.
- Draws each topology/material stream with a stable neutral shade so stage segmentation can be seen before texture decoding is implemented.
- Builds a deduplicated depth-tested wireframe edge buffer from the decoded 2,497 triangles and overlays it on the filled stage.
- Adds D4D near-plane and winding telemetry: triangles wholly before the near plane, near crossings, far rejects, in-depth triangles, and CCW/CW/degenerate winding counts.
- Clips diagnostic screen-bound calculations to the active near/far range so near-zero perspective divisions no longer explode telemetry into meaningless million-pixel bounds.
- Does not enable backface culling yet. v0.3.3 gathers the winding evidence first so the next pass can choose the correct orientation rather than risking a blind scene disappearance.

## Expected visual result
The stage should no longer read as one featureless flat slab if the topology is coherent. Individual surface groups and triangle edges should become visible. This is still an untextured diagnostic render, but it is intended to distinguish real floor/wall structure from bad topology immediately.

title: The stage was painting over the instruction to press OK
text:
# v0.3.4 device regression: stationary first stage

The input path preserves the native key masks, but the inherited final-frame compositor paints the GLES stage over the game's later 2D HUD and mission briefing. That briefing deliberately blocks player updates until the original Center/OK key is pressed. The normalized controls already included an OK button, but the covered briefing supplied no visible cue to press it. Ordinary directions and the four gameplay actions cannot dismiss that native gate.

[... selected excerpt ...]

## Why the prompt disappears

`bp.a(Graphics,i,ad)` uses this native paint order:

1. Android 2D clear/background.
2. GLES stage and player.
3. `Graphics3D.flushBuffer()` at bytecode offset 235.
4. `bh.a/b(Graphics,bn)` native HUD at offsets 240–273.
5. `k.b(Graphics,bn)` mission briefing at offset 293 when `k.d` is true.

`k.b` draws the briefing rectangle at `(6,83)` with size `228×64`; its text uses y=89,113,129. The old `RockmanCompat.flushBuffer` only captured the GLES frame. `RockmanCompat.unlock` later called `drawPostPresentGlFrame`, after the HUD/briefing had been painted. The merge loop unconditionally replaces every destination pixel whose captured GLES RGB exceeds the black-key threshold. Black-keying preserves only pixels where the GLES frame is black; an opaque gray stage overwrites later HUD and prompt pixels.

The correction merges GLES at the native flush boundary, after `endDrawing()` and before those HUD/script calls. Final unlock presents the already-composed frame. Native gameplay logic, payloads, model scale, camera, audio and saved assignments are retained. The existing normalized OK button continues to send the original Center bit.

title: An eight-degree turn became eight radians
text:
| Bytecode boundary | Evidence |
|---|---|
| Native `av.r()`, offsets 1170–1185 | Held Left calls `s.f(0,8,0)` and `h.g(0,8,0)`; Right at 1409–1424 uses -8. |
| Native `s.f(float,float,float)`, offsets 32–49 | Passes the raw Y angle to `Transform.rotate(Vector3D,float)` and multiplies the result into the native object transform. |
| Preserved host `Transform.rotate(Vector3D,float)`, code address `00b878` | Forwards the angle unchanged to the four-float overload. |
| Preserved host `Transform.rotate(float,float,float,float)`, code address `00b8a8` | At instruction offsets `0017–0021`, passes the raw angle directly into `Math.cos` and `Math.sin`. No degree conversion occurs. |

An intended native 8-degree turn therefore becomes 8 radians, equivalent to a 98.366-degree heading change modulo 360. That changes ordinary forward motion from a small curve into a mostly sideways displacement. The same mismatch also affects the guest's other raw degree rotations, including 90-degree commands.

The v0.3.6 math patch adds the conversion only inside `rotate`. It preserves the inherited 3×4 matrix indexing, local translate/scale, multiplication order, inverse, transpose, vector APIs and the current GLES-facing `lookAt` convention. It does not change controls, guest assets, collision logic or script gates. The two self-contained math classes must load in a parent of the preserved host/compatibility loader, ensuring that all layers share the same `Transform` and `Vector3D` types.

title: Shared model-format knowledge, distinct rendering paths
text:
## Models and animation

MbacMesh decodes original MB bone-local vertices, hierarchy, topology, per-corner UVs, material/texture slots, colors and appearance patterns. Texture decodes the original BMP resources used by Figure. Figure batches use original texture/material selection and upload to the preserved GLES1 backend; unavailable textures retain a defined geometry fallback.

ActionTable and MtraAnimation decode the original MT actions rather than supplying an empty duration. Action maxima and the guest's setTime remain Q16 frame values. Figure evaluates bone channels and composes them through the original hierarchy, applying the pose to the corresponding bone-local vertex ranges. Pose changes refresh the GLES vertex buffers; topology and source resources are retained. setAction starts the selected action at zero, and the guest then advances its own time. Animated appearance patterns follow the same action/time state. Monster Hunter supplied useful shared-format decoding knowledge; Rockman's presentation continues through ui.graphics3d/D4D/GLES rather than its incompatible opt.ui.j3d renderer.

title: Follow the original materials back to their images
text:
The native VertexBuffer descriptor references a signed-short, two-component UV array. Its UV bias is stored at descriptor offsets 52 and 56, and the scalar at 64. The decoded first `a1_3` UV is approximately `(0.9872478, 0.2206726)` using `bias + signed sample * scalar`. Coordinates outside `[0,1]` remain intact; the textures' authored repeat modes select GL_REPEAT. RGB or RGBA vertex arrays provide the stage's baked colors. Native triangle-strip lengths in this retained corpus are all three, so the previously rendered topology remains identical.

The decoder follows each Mesh topology/Appearance pair, its Texture2D reference, and its original Image2D reference. The game's converter has already changed the BMP palette from BGR to RGB and flipped the bottom-up BMP rows. Independent Python BMP decoding supplies a separate SHA-256 oracle for every selected texture, and the actual Group renderer's recorded GL uploads must match those original colors and row order. REPLACE materials with no alpha threshold render opaque; authored ALPHA/cutout materials retain their palette alpha. Native alpha thresholds, blend modes, depth test/write flags, and polygon offsets reach the GL submission path.

`python tests/check_world_materials.py` passed 591,498 parser/corpus checks and 814 actual Group GL submission assertions. These checks validate the original resource bytes, material references, buffers, GL state, texture reuse, and fallback bounds. They are JVM recording-sink checks, not Android/GPU or phone acceptance.

Known native water textures contain Texture2D AnimationTrack references. This pass retains and applies their stored constant UV transforms, records `animatedTexturesStatic`, and does not claim animated water UV tracks. Future unsupported material or object layouts have explicit diagnostic fallback. Supported native stages no longer receive the prior neutral shades and wireframe overlay.

## Audio evidence

Both MP4s contain an AAC track whose decoded samples are digital silence, so the recordings cannot verify audible balance, timing or music. The current runtime log does verify partial successful playback alongside codec rejection: 20 AUDIO PLAY and 17 AUDIO COMPLETE entries, plus 59 AUDIO ERROR entries. The inherited sound path therefore handles some sampled sounds while rejecting other native resources, including sequence-only music. title: The polygon reader and clipping shortcut could erase a model
text:
RENDERER CORRECTNESS CHANGES
A source comparison against the MIT-licensed MascotME MascotCapsule v3 implementation exposed two concrete mistakes/shortcuts in v0.0.4:

1. COLORED POLYGON BITSTREAM ORDER
MBAC colored polygons are stored as material -> vertex indices -> color index.
v0.0.4 consumed material -> color index -> vertex indices.
v0.0.5 consumes the original bitstream order while retaining our internal [material,color,index...] layout.

2. DEPTH-PLANE HANDLING
MascotCapsule behavior culls a triangle at the near plane only when all three vertices are behind it, and at the far plane only when all three are beyond it. Crossing polygons proceed to clipping.
v0.0.4 rejected a polygon if ANY vertex crossed either plane, which could erase entire models.
v0.0.5 stops discarding those crossing triangles. The current Canvas proof renderer uses the already near-clamped projected vertex as an approximation and records every crossing. Full attribute-preserving near/far clipping remains a later renderer step if the evidence says it is needed.

title: The characters and terrain were taking different routes
text:
Evidence from the physical v0.0.5 SM-S938U run:
- Game logic, HUD, enemies and hunter Figure models execute in hunt gameplay.
- Report recorded 1,394 Figure submissions and 289,967 drawn Figure triangles with no fatal exception.
- The world/terrain remained absent or appeared as diagnostic lines because renderPrimitives() still used the old fixed 2D wire proof and ignored the active view transform/projection.
- The game repeatedly constructed PrimitiveArray(4, 0x3000, 255) and PrimitiveArray(3, 0x0a00, 255). These values align with the MascotCapsule v3 data flags: texture coordinates (0x3000), per-face normals (0x0200), and per-face colors (0x0800). Therefore the actual constructor ABI is (primitive type, data flags, primitive count), not (type, count, flags).
- The v0.0.5 report also caught repeated Android IllegalStateException: Immutable bitmap passed to Canvas constructor for decoded GIF assets.

[... selected excerpt ...]

v0.0.6 changes:
1. Correct PrimitiveArray constructor semantics and buffer sizing.
2. Replace fixed wireframe renderPrimitives() with camera-aware projected triangle/quad rendering using the active view transform, perspective, center, clip, primitive texture selection, texture coordinates and per-face/per-command colors.
3. Preserve primitive render attributes used by MH i (lighting bit, color key, half/additive blend bits) for texture/blend behavior where currently supported.
4. Persist primitive counters in the exported REPORT so the next physical run shows submitted, queued, drawn, culled and crossing primitive geometry.
5. Convert decoded MediaImage bitmaps to mutable ARGB_8888 software bitmaps before creating the DoJa Image Graphics wrapper. This removes the repeated immutable-bitmap Canvas exception seen throughout the v0.0.5 report.
6. EN and JP game payloads remain unchanged.

This is still a proof renderer: full lighting, additive/subtractive blending, perspective-correct texture mapping, and full clipping remain future correctness work. The purpose of this pass is to restore the major missing PrimitiveArray world path and obtain a much more meaningful on-device scene/report.

title: A camera target had been treated as a direction
text:
Evidence from the v0.0.6 physical-device report:
- Figure renderer current-session geometry was entirely near-culled in the hunt.
- Last Figure: 589 vertices, 474 candidate polygons rejected at the near plane,
  transformed Z -818..-493 with near=128.
- Primitive path also near-culled 9935 of 11274 submitted primitives.
- No fatal exception occurred.

Root-cause audit:
Monster Hunter i's class b camera routine constructs two rotated offsets, then applies the SAME
world translation to both. It then calls AffineTrans.lookAt(j, k, up). That makes j a camera
world-space point and k a target world-space point. Treating k as a raw forward vector (the
v0.0.1-v0.0.6 implementation) is incompatible with the game's call pattern.

[... selected excerpt ...]

v0.0.7 changes:
1. com.nttdocomo.opt.ui.j3d.AffineTrans.lookAt now computes forward = target - position before
   building the view matrix. Degenerate target/up inputs throw, allowing the game's existing
   retry/catch path to behave meaningfully.
2. Graphics3D.setViewTrans snapshots the supplied matrix instead of retaining the caller's mutable
   object reference.
3. Persistent report adds view-call count, lookAt count, last view matrix, last lookAt
   position/target/forward, and a limited early stream of J3D VIEW / J3D LOOKAT records.
4. Figure/ActionTable parsing, EN/JP game payloads, saves, 2D image fix, and v0.0.6 PrimitiveArray
   renderer are otherwise unchanged.

[... selected excerpt ...]

External implementation note:
MascotME is valuable for MBAC/MTRA parsing and rendering behavior, but its generic
com.mascotcapsule.micro3d.v3 AffineTrans.lookAt accepts a look direction. Monster Hunter i is using
the older DoJa com.nttdocomo.opt.ui.j3d API in a target-point form, so directly transplanting that
single semantic would reproduce the v0.0.6 camera failure. The game's own bytecode is the stronger
compatibility oracle here.

title: The terrain’s materials and coordinates had their own rules
text:
Root-cause audit:
1. Primitive render attributes and Figure material flags are NOT the same bit layout.
   v0.0.7 passed the raw PrimitiveArray render-attribute integer into Figure material handling.
   In the old MascotCapsule primitive API used here:
     0x10 = color key
     0x20 = half blend
     0x40 = additive blend
     0x60 = subtractive blend
   Those values collide with unrelated Figure material bits. A hunt primitive using attrs=0x50
   therefore lost both its color-key and additive-blend intent in the bridge.

2. Primitive texture coordinates are texel-space values, not normalized 0..255 UVs.
   Monster Hunter i directly writes values such as 0, 32 and 64 into getTextureCoordArray(),
   including animated offsets. v0.0.7 incorrectly multiplied those coordinates by textureSize/256.

3. MascotCapsule sampling uses power-of-two backing dimensions. Some Monster Hunter textures are
   non-power-of-two logically (for example 256x240), so the bridge now pads the decoded indexed
   bitmap to the next power-of-two without rescaling the original image.

[... selected excerpt ...]

v0.0.8 changes:
- Translate PrimitiveArray PATTR bits into the bridge's internal Figure material representation.
- Honor primitive COLORKEY, HALF, ADD and SUB modes. SUB is an Android Canvas approximation
  (DARKEN) for now rather than a bit-exact subtractive software blend.
- For additive/subtractive indexed textures, palette index 0 is transparent when palette entry 0
  is black, matching the compatibility behavior used by the reference renderer.
- Sample primitive/model UVs directly in texel coordinates.
- Build power-of-two padded indexed texture bitmaps and retain logical dimensions separately.
- Extend REPORT with primitive material counters: textured, color-key, half/add/sub calls.

title: Sky holes, black fans, and the next three repairs
text:
Physical v0.0.8 evidence
------------------------
The SM-S938U run is now deep into real hunt rendering with recognizable hunter and Aptonoth models,
HUD, grass/path terrain pieces and animated combat. The persistent report recorded:
- Figure: 640 calls, 140621 queued triangles, 138358 drawn.
- PrimitiveArray: 2620 calls, 146854 queued triangles, 137772 drawn.
- Primitive near crossings: 3046.
- Primitive textured calls: 2470.
- No fatal exception and no missing texture objects.

The video still showed three characteristic renderer faults:
1. disconnected world chunks / large sky-blue holes despite large numbers of terrain triangles;
2. one-frame/angle giant black polygon fans near the camera;
3. textured terrain changing abruptly when animated/wrapped UVs crossed the 0/255 seam.

[... selected excerpt ...]

Root-cause audit
----------------
1. v0.0.8 rendered every Figure/PrimitiveArray Java call immediately and sorted only within that one
   call. MascotCapsule v3 accepts render commands but generates the pixels at flush(); the pending
   polygons can therefore be depth-sorted together. Monster Hunter itself uses several deliberate
   flush boundaries in the hunt renderer. v0.0.9 now preserves those boundaries and globally sorts
   all pending Figure + PrimitiveArray triangles inside each flush batch.

2. v0.0.8 only *pretended* to near-clip. A vertex behind the near plane was projected as if it sat on
   the near plane while the other vertices remained unchanged. Crossing triangles therefore became
   enormous fans/slabs. v0.0.9 performs Sutherland-Hodgman clipping against near/far Z planes,
   interpolates texture coordinates at clip intersections, triangulates the clipped polygon, and
   only then projects/culls it.

3. v0.0.8 byte-masked PrimitiveArray UVs with &255 before interpolation. Monster Hunter deliberately
   writes negative and >255 texture coordinates when scrolling/animating terrain. The reference
   MascotCapsule path keeps those integer coordinates continuous and converts them to fixed-point for
   rasterization; wrapping occurs while sampling. v0.0.9 keeps the raw signed integer UVs and lets
   the repeating texture shader wrap them after interpolation.

title: Restore contact behavior while keeping DeadShot’s own keys
text:
Purpose
-------
v0.0.9 keeps the v0.0.8 Dirge-style visual layout, but replaces the v0.0.8
free-sliding touch router with the known-good contact behavior taken from the
supplied Dirge Bridge v0.2.4 APK while preserving DeadShot's verified v0.0.5
native key map.

What changed
------------
- DeadShot key codes are unchanged from v0.0.5:
  keypad 1/2/3/4/6/7/8/9, *=10, #=11,
  D-pad 16/17/18/19, OK=20, Soft1=21, Soft2=22.
- A finger captures the control it starts on.
- Non-navigation buttons stay tied to that original control instead of turning
  into a neighboring button when the finger drifts.
- Navigation remains intentionally slideable so held movement can change direction.
- A small 4dp release/re-entry slop mirrors the supplied Dirge contact behavior.
- Multi-touch is aggregated before DeadShot receives key transitions, preventing
  duplicate presses/releases when two contacts resolve to the same native key.
- ACTION_DOWN requests that parent views do not intercept the control gesture.
- Releases are dispatched before replacement presses.
- No A/B/C aliases were introduced.
- Original DeadShot game JAR is unchanged.

title: DeadShot opens straight into the game
text:
Owner authorization: remove DeadShot's launch page for Omni integration, make
the original bridge follow the current gameplay-only pattern, preserve custom
controls, and proceed with the implementation after discussion.

## Implementation

GameActivity itself is the exported MAIN/LAUNCHER entry. It uses singleTop,
matching the repeated-entry policy in the inspected Dirge 0.3.0 manifest.
There is exactly one launcher filter and one real Activity. The former
LauncherActivity Java class and obsolete app ToolsActivity are removed.

An exported activity-alias named com.wakka.omnideadshot.LauncherActivity points
to GameActivity. Existing explicit component references can continue to enter
gameplay without executing a redirect Activity. The alias has no launcher
filter, so it does not add a second app icon. New callers can use GameActivity
or the package launch intent. There is no Android parent Activity or home page
to return to; system Back retains the existing input/audio/worker cleanup and
finishes gameplay, revealing its caller. Original Soft2 remains a game key.

The Rush Marine 0.0.9 device report is the reporting reference reviewed here. Its summary leads with live-session status, input press/release counts, interpreter/display counters, resource/audio outcomes and framebuffer results, followed by the retained trace. This pilot follows that structure using Snowboarding's available facts; it does not fabricate BREW counters in a DoJa game.

title: Rush Marine carries the work from DoJa into BREW
text:
Rush Marine Bridge is an independent Android compatibility bridge for running a user's own compatible copy of **Mega Man: Rush Marine**, the English **BREW 1.1.11 / CDM2030 128×160** release.

It executes the original game's **ARM/Thumb module** through a Java interpreter and supplies the BREW services that this title uses. The original game drives the gameplay.

[... selected excerpt ...]

## Why Rush Marine Bridge exists

Dirge, DeadShot, and FFVII Snowboarding were about making old DoJa games practical to play on modern Android. Rush Marine carries that bridge work into BREW.

The starting point was a preserved feature-phone package. Getting that package onto a modern phone meant making its original ARM instructions execute, supplying the phone services it expected, recovering its image and audio paths, and working out what its keypad events actually did.

This was developed through repeated chat-based AI iterations and testing on my phone. The reports and recordings mattered: things that looked correct on the host still broke on Android, and several assumed control mappings turned out to be wrong in real gameplay.

The working BREW runtime was then brought into the shared Wakkan/Omni bridge structure: a familiar front door, a larger game view, compact controls, and readable reports. This standalone public release adds local game-data import while retaining that baseline.

The original game and its preservation are separate from my bridge work. My aim here is to make the preserved game usable on modern Android.

title: The original module needs a real handset profile and timer
text:
## Evidence origin

The v0.0.1 physical S25 Ultra report proved the exact preserved module could load, construct class `0x01094C5E`, and accept `EVT_APP_START`. That report is retained under `evidence/device/`.

The v0.0.2 host investigation then followed the original executable one requested service at a time rather than inserting a synthetic framebuffer success path.

## Dependency chain observed

`module → applet → device info → persistent file → BAR resources/images → compatible bitmaps/display destinations → timer callback`

## Device information

The game constructor reads the handset dimensions through the shell. Leaving this structure zeroed caused an invalid negative allocation downstream. Supplying the preserved build's actual 128×160 profile removes that failure and advances the original code naturally.

[... selected excerpt ...]

## Display / bitmap path

The game queries image dimensions, asks the display for its destination bitmap, creates compatible bitmaps matching loaded image dimensions, switches display destination, issues image draw operations, then restores/switches destinations. v0.0.2 models those interface objects and preserves this control flow.

Current compatible bitmaps are structural HLE objects with width/height metadata. They do not yet contain/present authentic pixel backing.

## Timer path

The startup sequence schedules a 10 ms callback at `0x001131D8` with the applet pointer as callback data. v0.0.2 invokes one real scheduled callback after START. It executes **36,874 original instructions**, returns normally, and schedules another 10 ms callback.

title: The original code draws Enable Sound?
text:
The v0.0.2 S25 report exposed repeated display-interface calls during the first 10 ms timer callback. Rather than painting a Java replacement screen, v0.0.3 implements the behavior on the BREW host objects that the original executable is already calling.

## Pixel backing

Compatible bitmaps now own ARGB pixel arrays. PNG resources loaded from `mmassaultbacksmall.bar` are decoded through a platform hook and `IImage.Draw` blits those pixels into the currently selected BREW bitmap destination.

## Display calls

The repeatedly observed display `+0x14` call contains a pointer to four signed 16-bit values whose live values form sane in-bounds rectangles, followed by frame/fill color values and flags. v0.0.3 models that measured call as rectangle drawing. The timer-ending display `+0x1C` call is modeled as the frame update boundary.

The resulting output is not synthetic: executing the original timer code produces 432 rectangles over six updates and a coherent 128×160 screen reading **Enable Sound?**.

title: Twelve prefix bytes hide the sprites on Android
text:
## Device evidence that drove this pass

The returned v0.0.4 S25 Ultra report is a live Android 16/API 36 run. Its early BAR image path knows the original image dimensions but records `IImage.Draw ... pixels=no` for the resource-backed images. The preserved BAR resources are not raw PNG files: each of the four boot resources used in that path (`0x138E`, `0x1391`, `0x1394`, `0x13C0`) carries the same 12-byte resource prefix:

`0c 00 69 6d 61 67 65 2f 70 6e 67 00` = length + `image/png\0`

The real PNG signature begins at resource offset 12. Desktop `ImageIO` tolerated the prefix; Android `BitmapFactory.decodeByteArray` did not. That was the concrete reason the Android run showed rectangle/UI activity but not the real BAR sprite pixels.

The returned v0.0.4 recording separately proves the persistent input session is functional: the on-screen runtime counters reach thousands of display updates and hundreds of BREW key events, while the original menu reacts to keypad input. The saved text report, however, contains a clean 297,426-step/0-key snapshot rather than that later live session. v0.0.6 therefore also makes live-report capture occur before leaving the play surface and renames the destructive diagnostics action to make a fresh runtime reset explicit.

[... selected excerpt ...]

## v0.0.6 changes

1. **Android BAR PNG decode fix**
   - `BrewRuntime.makeImage` now locates the exact PNG signature inside the BAR resource and passes only the PNG stream to the platform decoder.
   - Image decode success/failure counters are included in the device report.
   - The host regression uses a deliberately strict decoder that rejects prefixed bytes, so this Android-specific failure mode cannot silently regress.

2. **Real held-key semantics**
   - Raw handset buttons now dispatch BREW `EVT_KEY_PRESS` on Android touch-down and `EVT_KEY_RELEASE` on touch-up/cancel.
   - The persistent 10 ms guest timer continues while a directional/action key is held.
   - This replaces the earlier atomic press+release click model while keeping `tapKey` as a desktop regression convenience.
   - Any held key is released when the activity pauses so the guest cannot be left with a stuck key.

3. **Report continuity**
   - The top-bar Report action snapshots the current persistent guest before opening Diagnostics.
   - Diagnostics labels a new-runtime action as `REBOOT RUNTIME (FRESH)` instead of an ambiguous generic probe.
   - Reports now include PNG decode counts and a compact count/last-location for unimplemented interface calls, which should make the next audio/display frontier easier to isolate.

title: The scrolling game is visible, and still silent
text:
## Physical v0.0.5 result
The returned S25 Ultra report remained live through 228,983,452 guest instructions, 5,296 display updates, 611,227 BitBlts, 19 successful BAR PNG decodes / 0 failures, and 228 live key events. This confirms the BAR pixel fix and persistent held-key event path on Android.

The returned screen recording visibly shows the game in live scrolling gameplay with character, enemies, clouds, water, terrain, HUD and sprite assets present. Its AAC audio track is digital silence (0.0 sample amplitude across the captured track), so there is still no audible output in this build.

title: The original HELP text describes the handset controls
text:
## Recovered original controls
The preserved BAR string/help resource states verbatim gameplay semantics:
- Move Up: Dpad-Up, 2
- Move Left: Dpad-Left, 4
- Move Down: Dpad-Down, 8
- Move Right: Dpad-Right, 6
- Move diagonally with 1, 3, 7, 9
- Fire: OK/5
- Toggle Auto-Fire: 0
- Pause: BACK
- Left softkey = OK; right softkey = BACK

v0.0.6 therefore stops asking the player to mentally translate a raw handset keypad during gameplay. The game-specific screen defaults to a labeled 8-way movement pad plus FIRE / OK, AUTO-FIRE, and GAME PAUSE / BACK. The complete raw keypad remains one tap away under the top Keypad toggle and stays the canonical BREW reference surface.

title: A RIGHT label that does not move right
text:
## Why this build exists

v0.0.7 proved the custom controls were mislabeled at the semantic layer. The host had assumed BREW D-pad alias values were trustworthy player-facing directions. The physical recording showed they were not: a button labeled RIGHT did not produce rightward movement, and gameplay could also enter an unwanted continuous-fire state.

## Changes

- Deleted the old custom direction mapping instead of trying to patch its labels.
- Player-facing directions now emit Rush Marine's documented numeric handset keys directly: **2 up, 4 left, 8 down, 6 right**.
- Diagonals emit **1, 3, 7, 9** directly; they are no longer synthesized from two alias keys.
- **FIRE** now emits original numeric **5**, not the assumed SELECT alias.
- **AUTO** emits original numeric **0** only on an explicit player tap. No startup or movement path sends 0.
- Kept the complete raw MGS-style handset keypad behind **Keypad** for reference/compatibility work.
- Kept the fixed, non-scrolling gameplay layout and added release checks preventing scrolling from returning.
- Removed the gameplay **Report** button. Diagnostics remain behind Bridgekeeper Tools; this control pass is validated by actual on-screen behavior, not by another report.

title: Measure movement instead of guessing key names
text:
The previous mapping inferred semantics from guessed BREW constant names and from hexadecimal suffixes. Both approaches were wrong.

A deterministic desktop A/B probe boots the original `mmassault.mod` to the same active gameplay state for every candidate, holds one guest key for 35 original timer ticks, then compares the player sprite position to a no-input control run.

Measured result:

- E031: dx=0, dy=-11 -> UP
- E032: dx=0, dy=+12 -> DOWN
- E033: dx=-13, dy=0 -> LEFT
- E034: dx=+12, dy=0 -> RIGHT
- E035 produces a fired projectile -> SELECT/FIRE
- E021 toggles continuous firing -> handset 0 / AUTO-FIRE
- E030 opens the original pause menu -> BACK/CLEAR

Original numeric aliases were also behaviorally confirmed: E022 up-left, E024 up-right, E028 down-left, E02A down-right. Disassembly around the held-key helper confirms 2/4/6/8 aliases E023/E025/E027/E029 for the four cardinals.

title: Two cardinal holds are not the game’s diagonal input
text:
## Physical v0.0.9 result

The returned S25 Ultra run confirms the v0.0.9 cardinal control correction worked physically. The remaining custom-control defect is limited to the four diagonal sectors: the raw keypad's 1/3/7/9 diagonal keys work, while the bespoke pad currently synthesizes two cardinal keys and the game does not treat that combination as its diagonal input.

The v0.0.9 device report also shows a healthy live runtime with 616 key events, 454,759,078 guest instructions, 11,121 display updates, 18/18 PNG decodes, zero unhandled interface calls, and an active guest/Android audio bridge.

## Diagonal correction

A deterministic guest A/B run proves the dedicated raw keypad diagonal codes directly move Rush diagonally:

- `0xE022` / keypad `1` = up-left (`dx=-13`, `dy=-11`)
- `0xE024` / keypad `3` = up-right (`dx=+12`, `dy=-11`)
- `0xE028` / keypad `7` = down-left (`dx=-13`, `dy=+12`)
- `0xE02A` / keypad `9` = down-right (`dx=+12`, `dy=+12`)

v0.0.10 therefore maps each bespoke diagonal sector to that one dedicated guest key. It no longer synthesizes two simultaneous cardinal holds.

title: Two long MIDI streams overlap before the first level
text:
## Startup audio overlap

The user's physical observation is that audio sounds strange just after the initial load/startup transition but sounds normal later in the level.

The guest-side timeline reproduces a concrete overlap risk:

1. The sound-enabled title/menu path plays BAR resource `0x232A` on one IMedia object.
2. Selecting START plays BAR resource `0x2335` on a second IMedia object.
3. Both payloads are Standard MIDI.
4. No guest Stop occurs between those two Play requests.

The exact preserved MIDI lengths are:

- `0x232A`: 51.1725 seconds
- `0x2335`: 35.0193 seconds
- later level music `0x2336`: 66.0 seconds

Android MediaPlayer permits the first two MIDI instances to coexist, which can create the startup overlap the physical run describes. v0.0.10 changes only host arbitration: starting a new Standard MIDI stream preempts any older Standard MIDI player, while QCP/SFX objects remain independent and may still overlap. No guest IMedia ABI, game bytes, rendering path, control cardinal mappings, viewport, Report flow, or launcher behavior is changed.

title: Replay the phone inputs to recover indexed geometry
text:
## v0.1.9 — original indexed 3D geometry

Replaying **all 28 original Zeebo HID button press/release events** from the physical S25 v0.1.8 report reproduced the exact GLES `0x0103D8DD + 0x140` fault at the Chapter 1 boundary. Three missing original GLES 1.x operations were then traced and implemented against Android's actual `GLES10` driver:

- **`+0x140 glMultMatrixx`**: original 16-element GLfixed matrix copied directly from ARM RAM; no substituted matrix.
- **`+0xDC glDrawElements`**: original unsigned-short or unsigned-byte indices read from ARM memory; the largest original referenced index is used to bound and pin the game's vertex and texture-coordinate arrays for the native GPU.
- **`+0xA8 glColorPointer`**: original per-vertex RGBA bytes copied from guest RAM and pinned for drawing. Also works with the previously implemented `glDrawArrays` path.

Unchanged original-game desktop replay now completes **500 native timer callbacks**, **497 GLES swaps**, **7,740 indexed geometry draws**, **7,740 matrix multiplications**, **215 vertex-color pointer calls**, **27 original texture uploads**, and **169 original file opens**, with **no guest execution fault**. Desktop test uses an ABI-counting graphics driver, not a real phone GPU. The Android version compiles and has a signed EGL14/GLES10 implementation of those calls.
note: The recorded replay uses an ABI-counting graphics driver on the desktop. It is not a new phone-GPU gameplay verdict.

- second tap: `Continue` -> `Attempting to initialize phone camera... Please wait...`

title: EOF was closing the Lua file after its first read
text:
## What actually unblocked New Game

The apparent missing room/pool initialization was downstream of a file callback error. The original user-filesystem registration puts **EOF at index2 and Close at index5**. The previous bridge treated these as reversed. Every EOF check therefore closed the Lua resource after its first 512-byte read. The remaining script, including the original `SetStart` call, never ran; current/requested room remained empty, room loading returned unchanged, and the original pools remained NULL.

Correcting that callback mapping allowed the original scripts to select/load FirstFloorUtility and initialize their own pools. The fix changes host routing; it does not insert a fabricated room name, scene, model, script result, or game-binary patch. `UserFileSystemContractProbe` passes **778 checks** against the original guest callbacks. Earlier NULL-pool traces are retained as discovery history, not the final runtime frontier.

title: The game handles unavailable camera hardware itself
text:
| Service | Actual behavior |
| --- | --- |
| Camera | Property0 reports unavailable; property1 returns measured initialization failure2. The original guest displays its failure page, updates its camera preference, and continues through its own fallback. No Android camera implementation or camera permission is claimed. |
| Secure storage | Get/Put success is0. The original opaque settings blob is retained, hashed, and restored with the requested exact size; failures remain errors rather than guessed settings. |
| User filesystem | Original all.dz callbacks are copied at registration; Open/Read/EOF/Seek/Tell/Close dispatch to the measured functions. EOF is2, Close is5. Host memory files support the measured read/write/position/EOF path. |
| User memory manager | s3eMemorySetUserMemMgr records original malloc/realloc/free callbacks; ordinary memory operations execute those original callbacks. Base allocation services retain their host implementation and avoid recursion into the guest manager. |
| Guest heap | A bounded reusable 16MiB arena replaces the nonreclaiming bump model. Host-reserved blocks are distinct from releasable guest blocks. Realloc preserves data; free allows reuse. Memory property2 is total remaining arena bytes; property4 is the largest aligned contiguous free block. |
| Zero-byte allocation | The original C++ allocator rejects NULL for zero-length arrays. A zero-byte guest request receives a unique releasable one-byte allocation. The original diagnostic path exposed the remaining-memory property2 requirement while correcting this behavior. |
| Keyboard | AnyKey returns an actual active key ID, which the original guest subsequently passes to GetState. KeyboardUpdate snapshots DOWN/PRESSED/RELEASED edges. ClearState clears consumed edges while retaining physical contact ownership. |
| Timing/lifecycle | Guest execution remains on MGS-Guest with cooperative yield. Foreground, window focus, and explicit Pause are independent; cancellation remains observable while paused. |

title: The phone asks for an audio channel the old tests missed
text:
## Device failure and coverage gap

The supplied Samsung SM-S938U Android16/API36 v15 report records 926 presents followed by `mem-read8-oob-0x000000FC`, 6144 submitted PCM samples and no Android-host failure. The supplied video contains silent decoded AAC. Its heap still has nearly15MB free, so the report does not indicate arena exhaustion. These exact inputs and their checksums remain under `evidence/device-v0.0.15-launch`.

The old CapturingMediaHost only demanded channel0 and discarded channel property2. Consequently earlier original-world/PCM tests did not run the channel1 decoder that the production Android sink requested on the phone. The old 16-byte generator descriptor overlapped the adjacent PCM buffer; original decoder0x00173FB5 reads source fields at16/20 and writes EOS at28. The main-loop PC0x0017B08E in v15 was restored after the nested fault, masking the actual callback location. v16 stores nested fault PC/state/registers before restoring the outer execution state.

Separate Android startup reasoning is independently reproduced by the sink contract: the old stream buffer was at least4096 mono frames, while demand stopped at3072 queued frames. Android's default API31+ stream start threshold is capacity. That queue can stay in startup underrun; the physical report itself did not record its actual head/threshold, so that precise device-side mechanism remains an inference. The new sink explicitly sets threshold1 on API31+ and measures per-channel head progress.

[... selected excerpt ...]

## Current measured audio contracts

Read `AUDIO_IMPLEMENTATION_v0.0.16.md` for original disassembly, source units and callback ABI. The descriptor is32 bytes: channel0, destination4, requested count8, mono flag12, original source16, source count20, unused/unconfirmed24 initialized0, output EOS byte28. Final positive PCM is submitted before EOS handling. Original repeat/loop metadata determines whether the source restarts or the sink stops demand and drains. Natural completion is delivered once, after consumed head reaches written samples; no final buffer is thrown away.

The original decoder resamples channel source-frequency property1 to global output-frequency property1. Generated AudioTracks therefore use the output rate; changing the source property does not retune already-resampled output. Global output-rate changes retune active generated tracks. Direct static PCM continues using its source rate. Existing source-frequency clamp4k..48k is retained. Channel/master gain application is retained; wider original volume behavior remains a future fidelity concern.

Modern steady demand remains1024 samples whenever the lead is below3072; the4096-frame stream buffer reserves one full chunk. Avoid tiny1–3-frame requests as the head advances. API26–30 cannot set the startup threshold, so they prime the effective full buffer. A finite source shorter than capacity is cached only during initial unconsumed startup and uploaded as exact static PCM. Static tracks start in STATE_NO_STATIC_DATA: upload must precede the initialized-state check. No padding or replacement sound is created.

Used-channel summaries retain accepted/nonzero/played counts, head, activity, guest pause, EOS, source/output rates, play count and threshold. Global counters retain master volume, lifecycle pause and failures. Accepted nonzero samples establish generated signal; head progress establishes AudioTrack consumption. Neither proves speaker output. Encoded MediaPlayer support remains separate from this original PCM path.

Do not treat compressed pixels as a CRC or exact guest histogram. title: Remove the title-artwork sleep from the scheduler
text:
The v17 phone report identifies a live scheduling defect rather than a stopped
guest. At present 2654, immediately after VIEW key 14, a first-person gameplay

title: Waiting for a handset state change
The first array repair
text:
Physical-device evidence from v0.0.4 reached the Japanese safety warning and Vivendi Games Mobile splash, then terminated in `c.x.b` with:

- backing array length: 49,216 integers
- attempted index: 98,296

Bytecode inspection of `c.x.b(int,int,int,int)` shows Chokkan calculates texture-coordinate offsets as `(PrimitiveArray.size() - 1) * 8` and writes eight integers per logical entry. For the observed logical count of 12,288, the final entry begins at 98,296 (`12,287 * 8`).

The bridge's earlier `PrimitiveArray` allocated `count * 4 + 64` integers for every backing array. With count=12,288 that is exactly 49,216, matching the physical-device exception.

v0.0.5 corrects the host compatibility layer rather than patching the game: vertex/normal/color storage permits 12 integers per logical entry, and texture/point-sprite storage permits 8. The logical `size()` remains unchanged.
note: Historical intermediate diagnosis, superseded by the constructor correction in CK05.

title: Why the first repair was incomplete
text:
## PrimitiveArray ABI correction

The actual constructor is `(type, flags, primitiveCount)`. The v0.0.5 host interpreted the second argument as the primitive count. Chokkan calls include `(4, 12288, 64)` and `(5, 4096, 1)`, so the earlier large allocations and size() results were wrong even after avoiding the immediate out-of-bounds access. This build interprets all three arguments correctly and supplies backing stores by the requested primitive topology.

## Rendering

The former renderFigure implementation counted calls without drawing. Primitive calls drew placeholder connected lines. The new host decodes real MBAC models and MTRA skeletal animation, transforms and projects the authored geometry, decodes texture atlases, and supports textured point sprites, quads and triangles. It preserves 2D/3D ordering and publishes a completed 240x320 frame to the UI.

## Input

Mappings come from original bytecode. Skydiving uses directional steering; sledding uses horizontal steering; dancing accepts directional combinations; hammer power responds to discrete key events on original STAR/POUND/0 keys; quiz answers use original1–9. Original gesture mode is selected through c.t's original setting methods on the game thread. Android accelerometer data replaces the old phone camera motion source. The guest's scene setup remains responsible for selecting roll or shake readers.

The guest active scene is a loop-local variable. Its pending scene field is cleared after entry and cannot drive an overlay reliably. Scene observation therefore uses each original scene's Frame.setBackground call. Original modal menus are separately recognized so directions and confirmation remain accessible.

[... selected excerpt ...]

## Completion scope

A clean original-game hammer run verifies repeated tap charging, setting power, angle selection and sustained flight with advancing fruit/distance counters. An earlier claimed result-screen check could not be corroborated by the final clean run and is excluded. Landing, results and full completion remain real-device tests.

text:
| Activity / original scene | Touch input | Original evidence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lobby (`lby.a`) | Left/right, SELECT | `b(c.f)` tests bits 16, 18 and 20. |
| Skydiving (`par.d` / `par.f`) | Four-way steering, OK | `par.f.a(c.f)` consumes held direction bits 16–19 and lets both axes work together. |
| Hammer throw (`ham.f`) | Repeated TAP presses, OK | `c.f.f()` increases power on keydown bits 10 (`*`),11 (`#`), or 0. `ham.f.b(c.f)` reads that power and uses bit 20 for power/angle timing. TAP alternates 10/11; holding does not generate repeated presses. |

| Dance (`dan.e` / `dan.c`) | Directional presses and diagonal chords, OK | KEY path `dan.c.b(c.f)` reads `c.f.i() & 983040` (bits 16–19), compares the exact chord, and advances the original prompt list. No invented dance action button. |

| Original options/dialogs | Four-way pad, OK, original soft labels | `c.f.ai == 0` signals the original modal UI. `c.f.F()` uses up/down for option rows, left/right for values, and bit 20 for confirmation. The pad replaces hammer/quiz controls while this modal UI is active. |

The lower soft keys retain original bits 21 and22. Their labels are taken from
`Frame.setSoftLabel` and translated only for known original labels. A blank
original label hides its button. This avoids presenting a guessed action.

[... selected excerpt ...]

## Motion

The TOUCH/MOTION switch requests the original global control option:
`c.t.c(2,1)` for KEY or `c.t.c(2,0)` for gesture. The request runs on the game
thread before its next keypad poll. `c.f.c(...)` starts the game's own roll or
shake reader for the current activity, rather than mapping accelerometer data
to fake keypad movement. Menu/skydiving/sled/dance use roll; hammer/quiz use shake.

The SH904i used camera motion tracking. Android supplies its accelerometer as
an adaptation of that sensing path. Recentered roll/pitch changes feed the
original `RollReader.getRollData()`; the game integrates those deltas, as its
bytecode specifies. Tilt sensitivity reaches the original ±120 range at
approximately 30 degrees from neutral. Filtered acceleration magnitude feeds
the original 0–511 `ShakeReader.getShakeData()` range. Touch pad deltas and
finite TAP pulses also feed these readers when motion mode is selected.

Recenter requests call the original `c.f.r()` on the game thread, clearing the
game's accumulated motion as well as the Android neutral point. Sensors stop
on pause. On resume, their first fresh gravity sample establishes a new neutral
before physical tilt contributes, preventing a phone moved in the background
from becoming an unintended steering command.

[... selected excerpt ...]

## Scene detection and interaction

The original game stores its active scene in a local variable; `c.f.p` is only
a pending transition and is cleared at entry. Each actual scene's entry calls
`Frame.setBackground`. That call's original stack identifies its class, and
`ControlProfile` reads its singleton for stage-specific labels. The exact FSM
fields are `par.d.p`, `ham.f.s`, `sno.d.o`, `dan.e.o`, and `sil.a.n`.

The viewport always preserves the complete 240×320 original surface. Controls
are below it, honor display insets, capture multiple fingers independently,
show pressed state, and release on cancel, focus loss, pause, or profile change.
Hardware directions/confirm are supported; X/Y map original `*`/`#` rhythm keys,
Start maps original softkey 1, and B maps original softkey 2. Digits map directly.

Desktop execution of the unchanged payload verifies these key/gesture paths.
Physical accelerometer feel and all five complete minigames still require
Android device testing. The report records scene, FSM stage, control mode,

title: Motion samples arrived; the game never read them
text:
The physical v0.0.6 report contains 11,472 accelerometer samples and seven mode changes, but zero RollReader polls. The host received phone motion; the original guest remained in its key-reader fallback.

## Cause

The original settings have a draft and a committed copy:

| Original API | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `c.t.l(2)` | Read draft control setting, used by the options display and some minigame logic. |
| `c.t.c(2, value)` | Write draft control setting. `0` is gesture, `1` is KEY. |
| `c.t.m(2)` | Read committed control setting, consulted by `c.f.c(int)` when selecting a reader. |
| `c.t.c()` | Original save/commit function, copying draft settings into the committed settings. |

v0.0.6 wrote and reported the draft setting without calling the original commit function. When the toolbar requested gesture mode, `c.f.c` still saw committed KEY mode and selected active reader `1`. The toolbar therefore said MOTION while the guest never called RollReader or ShakeReader.

## Repair

The Android toolbar writes the original setting, invokes the original save/commit function, and replays `c.f.z`, the original game's current reader request. That field retains the requested reader even when KEY mode falls back to reader `1`. This preserves the original requests for roll (`2`), shake (`3`), and the forced-gesture flag (`16`) used by motion practice, rather than selecting a reader from an overlay guess.

The mode display now follows committed `c.t.m(2)`. Reports include original requested and active reader values, RollReader poll count, ShakeReader poll count, and last sampled shake strength. The original save format and 4,096-byte scratchpad remain intact. The original commit function also commits any other draft options, matching the game's own options-close behavior.

The report's `Sensor neutral pending=true` occurred while the activity was paused for saving the report. `Paused: true`, PhoneSystem attribute 2 = 0, and the game thread waiting in `Host.awaitActive` corroborate that state. It is separate from the mode-commit defect.

[... selected excerpt ...]

## Verification

`MotionIntegrationProbe` executes the charset-compatible derivative of the original guest JAR against production bridge classes and Android API doubles. It feeds accelerometer events into `ChokkanInput`, lets the actual guest game loop poll its readers, and observes original guest fields. It does not invoke RollReader directly or supply steering/charge keys during the motion checks.

All five cases prove committed gesture mode, correct original active reader, sensor ingestion, persisted setting byte, and return to committed KEY mode. Skydiving, sledding, and dance prove signed left/right/forward tilt values through the original guest integration. Sledding additionally proves a change in the original player's world position. Hammer proves charge power from sensor shake; quiz proves the original reveal-strength field responds to sensor shake. The three roll cases also verify that a fresh sample after suspension becomes neutral without retaining earlier tilt.

title: Why decoded Japanese still broke its own wrapping
text:
## Japanese text

Video 00:00: lobby descriptions overflow the cream bubble. Video 00:26: `ロビーに戻りますか？` has a replacement character and choices below the cyan panel. Video 00:41: `もう一度、トライしますか？` is split into corrupted extra lines.

Original `c.j.a(String)` uses default-encoded bytes and fixed byte widths. The original CP932 encoding uses two-byte Japanese characters; Android UTF-8 uses three. Resource-only UTF-8 conversion allowed strings to decode, but subsequent byte wrapping split UTF-8 characters and made extra lines. Drawing-time replacement or Unicode width normalization cannot recover that layout correctly.

A reproducible build step translates eight default-charset String calls in five guest classes to explicit `windows-31j`. It changes only String encoding overloads. All 55 other classes and all resource entry bytes are copied exactly. The original JAR and DEX remain exact preserved assets; the loader runs a separate compatibility DEX. `Host.openJarResource` returns raw resource bytes, avoiding expanded tables overflowing the guest's fixed4,561-byte input buffer. `tools/TranslateGuest.java` and the included compatibility manifest document each translated call.

The original byte-based line widths, halfwidth characters, ASCII control markers and bitmap-font indices are retained. The return/retry panels should contain two lines; the skydiving lobby description should contain five lines instead of seven. No font size or guest coordinates are changed.

## Verification scope

Current test outputs are retained under `tests/text`, `tests/input` and `tests/runtime`. These execute the guest methods with Java/Android doubles; they do not substitute for testing the new tilt/shake feel on the S25 Ultra. The established renderer and audio implementations are unchanged. Full completion remains unverified.

TIMING / HEAT
- Original run() busy-waits without any sleep: backwards loops to bytecode13 until Diff-Timer >=100ms (bytecode51..73).
